prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type https://example.com/page into the address bar and press enter, the browser first has to decide whether what you typed is a URL at all or a search query, and once it has settled on a URL it parses the string into a scheme (https), a host (example.com), an optional port, a path, and any query string or fragment, with the scheme implying port 443 when none is given. Before any network traffic, the browser consults several local sources that may let it skip work entirely: its HTTP cache may hold a fresh copy of the resource, a service worker registered for the origin may intercept the request and answer from its own logic, and the browser's HSTS list may force an http:// request to be upgraded to https:// before it leaves the machine. If none of these answers the request, the browser needs an IP address for the host, and resolving the name is the first step that touches the network.

Name resolution proceeds through layers of caches. The browser keeps its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system's resolver, which consults the hosts file and its own cache before forwarding the query to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider, or in some browser configurations reached over DNS-over-HTTPS. If the recursive resolver has no cached answer, it walks the hierarchy by asking a root server which servers handle the top-level domain, asking those servers which nameservers are authoritative for example.com, and asking the authoritative server for the A record (IPv4) and AAAA record (IPv6). Each record carries a TTL that tells every cache along the way how long it may reuse the answer, which is why a DNS change at your provider takes time to be seen everywhere. Modern browsers often also query for HTTPS records, which can advertise support for HTTP/3 and other connection hints, and when both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses come back the browser races connections in a manner known as Happy Eyeballs, so that a broken IPv6 path does not stall the page.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this means TCP, which begins with the three-way handshake in which the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client answers ACK, costing one round trip before either side can send data. If the browser knows from an earlier visit, an HTTPS DNS record or an Alt-Svc header that the server speaks HTTP/3, it may instead use QUIC over UDP, which folds the transport and cryptographic handshakes together and saves round trips. Browsers also reuse connections they already have open to the same origin, in which case this step and the next are skipped completely.

Because the scheme is https, the connection must be encrypted and authenticated before any HTTP is sent, which is the job of TLS. In TLS 1.3 the client opens with a ClientHello listing the cipher suites it supports, a key share for a key exchange (typically elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), the Server Name Indication naming the host it wants so that a server hosting many sites on one IP knows which certificate to present, and ALPN identifiers such as h2 and http/1.1 so that the HTTP version is agreed during the handshake rather than in a separate exchange. The server answers with its own key share, which lets both sides derive shared symmetric keys, and then sends its certificate chain and a signature proving it holds the private key matching the certificate, all of it already encrypted. The browser validates the chain by checking that each certificate is signed by the next up to a root authority in the operating system or browser trust store, that the dates are valid, that the hostname matches one of the names in the certificate's subject alternative names, and that the certificate has not been revoked, a check browsers usually make against compact built-in revocation lists rather than by contacting the authority on every visit. If any of this fails, the browser shows a certificate error instead of continuing. When validation succeeds, both sides send Finished messages, and a full TLS 1.3 handshake needs only one round trip, down from two in TLS 1.2; on a return visit, resumption using a ticket from the earlier session can shorten things further, and with 0-RTT the client may even send its request alongside its first flight, at the cost of replay risk that limits this to safe requests.

Only now can the browser send the HTTP request, which it does through the encrypted channel. In HTTP/1.1 the request is text, a request line such as GET /page HTTP/1.1 followed by headers like Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding and any cookies stored for that domain, while in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information is encoded into binary frames with compressed headers, the host appearing as the :authority pseudo-header and many requests able to share the one connection. The request often does not go straight to the machine that runs the application, since it commonly reaches a CDN edge or a load balancer first, which terminates TLS, may answer from its cache, and otherwise forwards the request to an origin server, perhaps over another connection with its own handshake. The origin server routes the request to application code, which might query a database, render a template or read a file, and then begins writing a response, status line and headers first, with the body following.

The first byte of that response arriving at the browser, which performance tools report as time to first byte, is therefore the sum of everything above: any redirect hops, the DNS lookup, TCP or QUIC connection setup, the TLS handshake, the time the request takes to cross the network, the server's own processing time, and the time for the first byte to travel back. Developers tune these parts separately, using DNS caching and preconnect hints for the early stages, keep-alive and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for connection reuse, and server-side caching or a CDN for processing time and distance. Redirects deserve particular attention because a request for http://example.com or for a non-canonical hostname commonly receives a 301 or 302 pointing elsewhere, and each one restarts much of this process for the new URL, so a single redirect to a different host can roughly double the connection cost before the real response begins.
